title: Inside the Container: `docker exec` & Interactive Mode 🎮
description: Learn to run commands inside a running container and open interactive shells.

slides.title: Why Enter a Running Container? 🚪
slides.content:
# Containers Are Like Apartments

You can look at them from the outside (`docker ps`, `docker logs`), but sometimes you need to **go inside** to:

- Debug a running application.
- Check file contents or environment variables.
- Run diagnostic commands (e.g., `ps`, `ls`, `curl`).
- Install temporary tools (not recommended for production, but useful in development).

Docker gives you two main ways: **`docker exec`** (the right way) and `docker attach` (the old way).

slides.title: `docker exec` – Run Any Command 🏃
slides.content:
# Syntax

```bash
docker exec [OPTIONS] CONTAINER COMMAND [ARG...]
```

This runs a **new process** inside the container’s namespace. The container must be running.

**Examples:**
```bash
docker exec my-nginx ls /usr/share/nginx/html
docker exec database psql -U postgres -c "SELECT 1"
```

The command runs and the output appears in your terminal.

quizData.question: What must be true for `docker exec` to work?

options.text: The container must have SSH installed.

quizData.explanation: `docker exec` launches a new process in a running container. If the container is stopped, it can’t execute anything.

slides.title: Interactive Shell: `-it` 🤖
slides.content:
# Getting a Shell Inside a Container

Combining flags `-i` (interactive) and `-t` (allocate a pseudo‑TTY) gives you a full terminal experience.

```bash
docker exec -it my-container bash
```

- `-i` keeps STDIN open.
- `-t` provides a terminal driver (so you can use `clear`, get coloured output, etc.).

If the image doesn’t have `bash`, try `sh`:
```bash
docker exec -it my-container sh
```

Now you’re “inside” the container. Run commands like you would on a normal Linux machine. Type `exit` to leave.

slides.title: Live Demo 🎬
slides.content: Start a container and get inside:
slides.codeSnippet:
# Start a long‑lived container
docker run -d --name sandbox alpine sleep 3600

# Open an interactive shell
docker exec -it sandbox sh

# Inside the container
ls -l
echo $PATH
ps aux
exit  # go back to host

quizData.question: What is the purpose of the `-t` flag in `docker exec -it`?

options.text: It allocates a pseudo‑TTY for a proper terminal interface.
It runs the command as root.
It terminates the container after the command finishes.

quizData.explanation: `-t` stands for TTY. Without it, many interactive programs would misbehave. Combine with `-i` for a full shell.

slides.title: Which Shell to Use? ⚠️
slides.content:
## Not all images have bash!

- **Alpine** images use `sh` (busybox ash).
- **Ubuntu/Debian** usually have `bash`.
- **Minimal images** may have no shell at all!

Always check the image documentation. Try `sh` if `bash` fails.

slides.title: Running Commands as Another User 👤
slides.content:
# `--user` Flag

By default, `docker exec` runs commands as the container’s default user (often `root`). You can change it:

```bash
docker exec -u www-data my-nginx whoami
```

This is critical for security – avoid running as root inside containers when unnecessary.

quizData.question: How do you run a command inside a container as the user `nobody`?

options.text: Both b and c are correct

quizData.explanation: Both `-u` and `--user` work, but `-u nobody` is the short form. The option expects a username or UID.
